title: Designing Custom Event Systems
subtopics: When direct function calls are better than events
learning_outcomes: Describe Custom event names and explain how it relates to Designing Custom Event Systems.
Demonstrate Event payload design in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Internal application events.

content.intro: Designing Custom Event Systems is part of events and event driven programming. This lesson connects Custom event names, Event payload design, Internal application events to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Event-driven code separates the producer of a change from listeners that react to it. Test listener order, one-time listeners, duplicate subscriptions, and error-event behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Event-driven code separates the producer of a change from listeners that react to it. Define stable event names and payload contracts, handle error events, and remove listeners when their work ends.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Designing Custom Event Systems. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Custom event names; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming EventEmitter listeners are asynchronous or leaving listeners attached for longer than intended.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Remember emission is synchronous by default and manage listener lifetime explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
